blocks.title: Orientation, authorization, and learning habits
blocks.outcome: explain what a penetration test is and create the records needed to practice responsibly. Learn concepts here; install the lab in Block 01.

blocks.title: Computer literacy and an isolated lab
blocks.outcome: use a computer confidently and explain what is happening when software runs. Do not begin with attack tools.

blocks.title: Networking from first principles
blocks.outcome: explain a request from application to destination, interpret packets, and troubleshoot connectivity.

blocks.title: Linux administration and the command line
blocks.outcome: understand the operating system beneath the tools. Use Ubuntu first; introduce Kali as a toolbox after you can manage a normal Linux guest.

blocks.title: Windows, PowerShell, and endpoint internals
blocks.outcome: administer and inspect a Windows lab without confusing local accounts, administrator rights, and domain identities.

blocks.title: Programming, automation, and reproducibility
blocks.outcome: write and debug small tools, read unfamiliar code, and understand what a downloaded script will do before running it.

blocks.title: Build applications before testing them
blocks.outcome: understand the browser, server, database, and identity boundaries that create application vulnerabilities.

blocks.title: Security principles, cryptography, and defense
blocks.outcome: explain why a weakness matters and how a control addresses it, rather than identifying tools by name.

blocks.title: A repeatable penetration-testing method
blocks.outcome: move from a written scope to a defensible finding. Learn why and when to use a tool before relying on its output.

blocks.title: Core web application vulnerabilities
blocks.outcome: discover and explain common application flaws manually. For a video embedded under a lab's **Community solutions**, treat that lab as a demonstration. Attempt it first, then watch; use a different lab for your independent task count. Never count a watched solution as an unseen solve.

blocks.title: APIs, advanced web behavior, and code review
blocks.outcome: investigate state, identity, and parser interactions that simple scanners frequently miss. Read research papers critically and reproduce only their designated lab scenarios.

blocks.title: Network services, host access, and privilege escalation
blocks.outcome: reason from exposed service to authorized proof, understand privilege boundaries, and assess reachable lab segments without treating a tool's success message as sufficient evidence.

blocks.title: Active Directory and identity attack paths
blocks.outcome: understand how enterprise identity relationships create access paths and how to remove those paths. This is a substantial engineering topic, not a list of attack commands.

blocks.title: Cloud, containers, and software delivery
blocks.outcome: reason about identities, policies, workloads, and secrets across modern infrastructure. Start with one provider in depth—AWS here—and learn to translate the model to Azure/Entra and GCP. Breadth alone is not multi-cloud expertise.

blocks.title: Reverse engineering and vulnerability research
blocks.outcome: understand executable behavior, investigate crashes, and distinguish a reproducible bug from a proven security vulnerability. This block introduces advanced research foundations; kernel, browser, hypervisor, and firmware exploitation remain additional specialties.

blocks.title: Independent engagements and professional delivery
blocks.outcome: plan, execute, and communicate an assessment another professional can trust. This is the core graduation block.

blocks.title: Mobile application specialization
blocks.outcome: practical Android assessment plus an informed iOS comparison. iOS hands-on completion requires suitable Apple hardware/software and, for some techniques, suitable test-device access; do not claim it from Android-only work.

blocks.title: Wireless and IoT specialization
blocks.outcome: assess wireless configurations and embedded-software attack surfaces. Use supplied captures or your own access point; active interference with nearby networks is outside this curriculum.

blocks.title: AI application security specialization
blocks.outcome: assess an AI-enabled application's data access and actions. This is application security around probabilistic components; making a chatbot say something surprising is not automatically a security finding.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 00 — Permission and practice plan

quizQuestions.prompt: A company publishes its IP address. What additional condition must be met before you test it?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Explicit authorization from an appropriate owner and scope covering the asset and proposed actions; visibility alone grants nothing.

quizQuestions.prompt: How does a penetration test differ from simply running a vulnerability scanner?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A test uses a defined scope, manual validation, impact analysis, and reporting; a scanner provides candidate findings, including mistakes.

quizQuestions.prompt: A permitted application redirects to an external identity provider. What should you do?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Stop at that boundary unless the separate service is explicitly authorized; clarify with the owner.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the difference between an observation and a hypothesis? Give an example.
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: “The response is 403” is an observation; “the role check caused it” is a hypothesis that needs a controlled test.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is a VM snapshot useful, and what does it not replace?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: It enables rollback of guest state; it does not replace independent backups, isolation, or evidence records.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should you record unsuccessful tests?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: They show coverage, prevent repeated dead ends, and constrain conclusions about what was actually tested.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: submit the Cedar Lab authorization sheet, diagram, notebook sample, and ten scope decisions. Score: **scope completeness / isolation reasoning / reproducible notes / correct boundary decisions**. Pass using the universal rules before installing the practice lab.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 01 — Rebuildable workstation

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does adding disk space not necessarily fix a machine running out of RAM?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: RAM holds active working data; disk capacity is a different resource. Paging may help capacity but can be much slower.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does an operating system provide that an ordinary application does not?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: It manages hardware, processes, memory, files, and access between programs and devices.

quizQuestions.prompt: Is renaming `picture.jpg` to `picture.txt` a conversion? Explain.
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: No. The bytes and format stay the same; only the name changes.

quizQuestions.prompt: Which two machines are meant by “host” and “guest”?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The host runs the hypervisor; the guest is the OS inside a virtual machine.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is NAT alone insufficient to guarantee a vulnerable guest cannot reach other systems?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: NAT commonly permits outbound traffic and may have port forwards; verify routes and interfaces and use stronger lab separation.

quizQuestions.prompt: What must you record so another learner can recreate your VM?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Image/source and version, architecture, virtual resources, network mode, setup steps, and recovery/verification procedure.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: rebuild a guest from your instructions, recover a file, demonstrate snapshot rollback, and explain its connectivity. Score: **working rebuild / data recovery / isolation verification / hardware-and-OS explanation**.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 02 — Explain the packet journey

quizQuestions.prompt: What does a switch normally use to forward an Ethernet frame? What does a router use?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Destination MAC and its forwarding table; destination IP and the routing table respectively.

quizQuestions.prompt: For `192.168.10.70/26`, give network, ordinary usable range, and broadcast.
A hostname fails but an IP connection works. What is one reasonable hypothesis and test?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: DNS resolution may be wrong; inspect resolver configuration and compare the name's answer with the intended IP.

quizQuestions.prompt: Does an open TCP port prove that a service is vulnerable?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: No. It indicates a listener; vulnerability requires further evidence of a weakness under relevant conditions.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does TLS protect, and what does it not establish about application authorization?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: It protects transport confidentiality/integrity and supports endpoint authentication; it does not decide which records a logged-in user may access.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can a machine that ignores ping still provide a working web service?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: ICMP may be filtered while TCP/HTTPS is allowed; different protocols have different policies.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: deliver a two-subnet diagram, ten correct subnet calculations after corrections, annotated captures, and diagnosis of three faults. Score: **addressing / packet interpretation / systematic troubleshooting / correct trust-boundary explanation**. Network+ preparation becomes plausible later after the certification gap checklist.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 03 — Operate without a walkthrough

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can a user read a file but still fail to access it through a directory?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Traversing directories requires appropriate execute/search permission along the path, in addition to the file's permissions.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does `sudo` change about a command's execution?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: It runs the permitted command under another identity, usually root, according to policy; it is not a universal requirement.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can a tool available in one terminal be “not found” in another?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: PATH, environment, shell initialization, working directory, or installed environment may differ.

quizQuestions.prompt: How do stderr and an exit status differ?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: stderr carries diagnostic text; exit status is a process result code. Either can exist without a useful message in the other.

quizQuestions.prompt: What risk does accepting an unexpected SSH host-key change create?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: You might trust an impersonating host; verify the legitimate host's fingerprint through a trusted channel.

quizQuestions.prompt: A service has stopped. What evidence should you collect before reinstalling it?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Status, recent logs, configuration validity, resource use, dependencies, and recent changes; preserve the error before changing state.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: from a clean guest, build the two-user permission model, install/restrict a service, diagnose a planted failure, and restore it. Score: **shell fluency / access correctness / evidence-led diagnosis / recovery**.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 04 — Windows administration evidence

quizQuestions.prompt: Why might access through an SMB share fail even when NTFS permissions appear sufficient?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Share permissions, identity, firewall/network policy, and NTFS permissions all matter; effective access depends on the actual path and identity.

quizQuestions.prompt: How is the PowerShell pipeline different from an ordinary text pipe?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Cmdlets commonly pass structured objects with properties, not only displayed strings.

quizQuestions.prompt: Does membership in Administrators mean every process runs elevated?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: No. UAC and token/elevation context affect the running process.

quizQuestions.prompt: What information can a process tree reveal that a filename alone cannot?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Parentage, command-line context, user identity, and related child activity support a more reliable interpretation.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does the absence of a login event not prove no login occurred?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Auditing may be disabled, logs may have rolled over, or the event may be elsewhere; check collection coverage.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should a collection script distinguish “zero results” from “access denied”?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Missing visibility is not evidence of absence. Reporting the error preserves the validity of the assessment.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: deliver your inventory script, two-user access matrix, annotated process evidence, and login-event timeline. Score: **permissions / useful automation / event interpretation / recovery and limitations**.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 05 — Build a dependable small tool

quizQuestions.prompt: How do bytes differ from a Unicode string when communicating over a socket?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Sockets transfer bytes; strings require a defined encoding/decoding. Confusing them causes errors or data corruption.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can an HTTP timeout not be reported as status code 200?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: No successful HTTP response was observed; report a connection/request error, not invented evidence.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is one boundary case for a log parser, and why does it matter?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Examples include empty input, malformed timestamps, or unexpected encoding; mishandling can distort conclusions or crash the tool.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should a network tool have both a timeout and a request limit?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A timeout bounds waiting per operation; a limit bounds workload and overall effect. Neither fully replaces the other.

quizQuestions.prompt: A password was committed and then deleted. Is the repository safe to share?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Not necessarily: history may retain it. Rotate any real secret and review/remove exposure before sharing.

quizQuestions.prompt: What makes a bug report reproducible?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A minimal input, environment/version, exact steps, expected and actual result, and supporting evidence.

practicalCriteria.label: Error handling and tests
practicalCriteria.description: Assessed as: error handling and tests.

practicalCriteria.label: Documentation and clean rebuild
practicalCriteria.description: Assessed as: documentation and clean rebuild.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: independently build a lab inventory/report generator combining a local file parser and bounded HTTP checker. Score: **correct outputs / error handling and tests / scope controls / documentation and clean rebuild**. Do not progress if you cannot explain your own code.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 06 — Explain your own application

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is hiding an administrator button insufficient access control?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Clients can send requests without the interface; enforce permissions on the server for every relevant operation.

quizQuestions.prompt: How does a session cookie differ from the server-side session data it references?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A cookie is browser-held data; in a server-side session design it often identifies state stored separately. Other session designs exist.

quizQuestions.prompt: What separates authentication from authorization?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides permitted actions on specific resources.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why are parameterized database queries safer than concatenating user input?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Values are handled as data rather than changing query structure, when the API is used correctly.

quizQuestions.prompt: Can a frontend API key be treated as a secret? Why?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Generally no: users can inspect delivered code/network traffic. Restrict public identifiers and keep actual secrets server-side.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why must an API check ownership even when object IDs are hard to guess?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Unpredictability is not authorization; leaked or discovered IDs must not grant access across users.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: demonstrate the notes application and API, explain one full request's path, show cross-user denials, and rebuild from documentation. Score: **working system / correct identity boundaries / protocol-and-data explanation / tests and reproducibility**.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 07 — Defend the system you built

quizQuestions.prompt: Give different examples of a threat, a vulnerability, and a risk for the notes app.
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: An unauthorized reader is a threat actor/capability; a missing ownership check is a vulnerability; confidential notes being exposed is a risk scenario.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is Base64 unsuitable for protecting a password?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: It is reversible encoding with no secret key, not password storage protection.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does a password salt accomplish, and what does it not accomplish?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Unique salts make identical passwords differ and hinder precomputed comparisons; they do not replace a slow password KDF or strong passwords.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does MFA not fix a missing record-ownership check?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: MFA strengthens identity verification; the application must separately authorize access to each object.

quizQuestions.prompt: Who normally decides permissions on customer data stored in a cloud service?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Responsibility depends on the service, but customers commonly configure their identities and data access; the provider does not make every authorization decision for them.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should a backup be restored during testing rather than merely checked for existence?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Existence does not prove integrity, completeness, available keys, or a working restoration process within the required time.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: deliver the threat model, working controls, restored backup, and incident tabletop record. Score: **risk reasoning / correct cryptographic choices / defense-and-recovery validation / clear communication**. You now have foundations for CC/Security+ preparation; use the current-objective gaps in the certification section.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 08 — A small complete assessment

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the difference between recon and vulnerability validation?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Recon discovers assets/behavior; validation tests a specific security hypothesis and its preconditions.

quizQuestions.prompt: A scanner reports a CVE based on a banner. What must you check next?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Actual version/build, patch backports, configuration, exposure, and safe reproduction against the affected condition.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can authenticated testing reveal weaknesses missed by an unauthenticated scan?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Privileged features, role boundaries, and logged-in workflows may not be visible otherwise.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is a false positive? Give a plausible example.
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A reported weakness that is not present; for example a version-only alert where the vulnerable code was backport-patched.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can two businesses assign different priority to the same technical vulnerability?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Data sensitivity, exposure, business dependency, compensating controls, and threat context differ.

quizQuestions.prompt: What evidence belongs in a retest record?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The changed version/configuration, repeated original test, negative/positive controls, result, date, and any remaining limitation.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: assess your app and one lab service under a written scope; submit an inventory, test log, validated findings, and retest. Score: **coverage / validation quality / impact and remediation / reproducible report**.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 09 — Unlabeled web assessment

quizQuestions.prompt: A user can change a record ID and read another user's note. Which control failed?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Object-level authorization/ownership enforcement, not necessarily authentication.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is SQL injection not fixed reliably by merely removing quote characters?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Query contexts, encodings, and syntax vary; use parameterized access and appropriate structural controls.

quizQuestions.prompt: How does stored XSS differ from reflected XSS?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Stored input is retained and later rendered; reflected input appears from the current request. Both require an unsafe output context.

quizQuestions.prompt: Explain one important distinction between XSS and CSRF.
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: XSS executes attacker-controlled content in a trusted context; CSRF induces an authenticated action through ambient browser credentials, often without reading the response.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can an SSRF flaw reach a service that your browser cannot reach directly?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The server issues the request from its own network and identity context, crossing a different boundary.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does checking an upload's extension alone provide weak protection?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Names are attacker-controlled and may not match content; storage/execution configuration and robust validation also matter.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: in your local [Juice Shop][JUICE] or [WebGoat][WEBGOAT], identify and validate at least five findings across four vulnerability families without using challenge solutions. Include one rejected candidate and fixes/retests for two classes in your own app. Score: **independent discovery / accurate causes / evidence and impact / remediation and retest**. Finish a minimum of **30 independent core-web lab solves** across the block; extras may come from [Natas][NATAS] or [Hacker101 CTF][H101CTF].
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 10 — Think beyond vulnerability names

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is decoding a JWT different from verifying it?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Decoding reads data; verification checks authenticity and relevant claims using the intended trust configuration.

quizQuestions.prompt: A GraphQL endpoint requires login. Why may field-level data still leak?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Authentication at the endpoint does not guarantee authorization in each resolver/object/field.

quizQuestions.prompt: What distinguishes cache poisoning from cache deception?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Poisoning influences a cached response delivered to others; deception causes sensitive responses to be cached under an inappropriately reusable location/key.

quizQuestions.prompt: What must disagree for a request-smuggling hypothesis to make sense?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Components sharing a connection must parse request boundaries or routing differently; mere unusual formatting is insufficient proof.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can two individually valid requests violate a rule when run concurrently?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Both may observe the same precondition before either updates state; an atomic invariant is missing.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is a static-analysis warning not automatically a confirmed vulnerability?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Reachability, attacker control, sanitization, configuration, and impact must be verified.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: complete a second application/API assessment and **25 independent advanced labs**, including at least one from every family above. Deliver a role/endpoint matrix, two safe multi-step chains, one source-based fix, and a retest. Score: **coverage across interfaces / chain correctness / controlled proof / actionable report**. Aim for 60+ total web/API solves before considering a web certification; certification readiness additionally needs its own practice criteria.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 11 — An unfamiliar host assessment

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is an exploit for a product name alone insufficient evidence it will work?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Version, patch, architecture, feature, authentication, and configuration conditions must match.

quizQuestions.prompt: What distinguishes a local privilege escalation from an initial-access vulnerability?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Escalation crosses a privilege boundary after an existing foothold; initial access creates the first relevant access path.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does a readable hash not necessarily reveal a plaintext password?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Hashes/KDF outputs are not reversible encryption; candidates must be tested, and cost/entropy matter.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why are offline password recovery and online login guessing operationally different?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Offline tests use owned hash samples without service requests; online attempts interact with account controls, lockouts, and monitoring.

quizQuestions.prompt: What changes about network reachability when you use a permitted pivot host?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Connections originate or route through a new authorized context; that does not expand the engagement's permitted targets.

quizQuestions.prompt: What must you document before reverting a vulnerable VM?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Starting/ending identity, reproducible steps, evidence, affected state, cleanup performed, and important limitations.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: complete **four distinct lab-host assessments**: two Linux and two Windows configurations, including low-privilege access, escalation, and one multi-segment path across the set. At least two must be unfamiliar challenges or configurations selected by a peer. Score: **enumeration / independent validation / privilege-and-network explanation / reporting and cleanup**. If Windows licensing or hardware prevents this, keep this gate incomplete; a Linux-only substitute does not demonstrate Windows competence.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 12 — Assess an identity path, not a diagram

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can broken DNS or clock skew disrupt domain authentication?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Domain services rely on name/service discovery, and Kerberos relies on bounded time differences for ticket validity.

quizQuestions.prompt: How does a local administrator differ from a domain administrator?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Local authority concerns a specific computer; domain-level rights can affect directory objects and many systems, depending on policy.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is a BloodHound path a hypothesis rather than unconditional proof of compromise?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Collection may be stale or incomplete, and connectivity, tokens, configuration, or protections may block the path.

quizQuestions.prompt: How does relaying authentication differ from cracking a password hash?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Relay forwards an authentication exchange to another accepting service; cracking tests candidate secrets offline. Their prerequisites and defenses differ.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can a certificate-template permission become an identity-security issue?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A template may permit obtaining an authentication certificate representing an unintended identity or purpose.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why must an identity fix be retested with fresh collection and actual access checks?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Old graphs and cached permissions may mislead; verify both the relationship data and the behavior the fix is intended to stop.

practicalCriteria.label: Practical mitigations and retests
practicalCriteria.description: Assessed as: practical mitigations and retests.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: perform an assumed-breach assessment from an ordinary lab account. Validate two distinct paths to a designated high-value test resource, including one rights/configuration path; demonstrate a certificate-related finding where supported. Submit a full report and a 15-minute recorded debrief. Score: **identity understanding / independently validated paths / practical mitigations and retests / debrief and evidence**. Passing supports further PNPT/CRTP/CPTS preparation; it is not automatic exam eligibility.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 13 — Cloud and workload trust

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is a temporary credential still dangerous when its permissions are excessive?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: It can exercise those rights until expiry or effective revocation; lifetime and authorization are separate controls.

quizQuestions.prompt: What two sides of a cross-account access relationship may require configuration?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The requesting identity's permissions and the target's trust/resource policy, subject to relevant boundaries and organizational controls.

quizQuestions.prompt: Does a Kubernetes namespace automatically provide complete tenant isolation?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: No. RBAC, network, workload, node, and other controls must support the intended isolation.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can mounting a container-management socket defeat the intended container boundary?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Access to a sufficiently privileged daemon may allow control over containers or the host; the socket is a sensitive administration interface.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should untrusted pull-request code not receive deployment secrets?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The code could read or misuse them; event context, token permissions, and workflow trust must be constrained.

quizQuestions.prompt: What competence is not proved by reviewing cloud policies entirely offline?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Real provider deployment, troubleshooting, logging configuration, cleanup, and operational test behavior remain unproven.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: submit the corrected policy bundle with reasoning, local container/Kubernetes assessment, synthetic audit analysis, and CI review. Score: **identity-policy correctness / workload boundary validation / evidence and logging / supply-chain controls**. Label this **offline/local cloud-security foundation** unless you also complete and document live-provider practice.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 14 — Prove what your research supports

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the difference between a pointer and the value stored at its address?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A pointer represents an address; dereferencing accesses the object at that location, subject to validity and type rules.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why can decompiled code disagree with the original source while still approximating behavior?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Compilation removes or transforms names, types, and structure; the decompiler infers an approximation from machine code.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does one crashing input not prove reliable code execution?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Exploitability depends on controlled state, useful primitives, protections, reliability, and reachable conditions.

quizQuestions.prompt: How do ASLR and non-executable memory address different parts of exploitation?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: ASLR changes relevant addresses; NX/DEP restricts execution from designated memory regions. Neither repairs the original bug.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why minimize a crashing test case?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A small reproducer isolates the trigger, simplifies debugging, and improves reliable regression testing.

quizQuestions.prompt: What should you conclude when a fuzzing run finds no crashes?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Only that the tested configuration/corpus/budget revealed no crash; absence of findings is not proof of absence of vulnerabilities.

practicalCriteria.label: Patch and honest limitations
practicalCriteria.description: Assessed as: patch and honest limitations.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: deliver a research dossier with a C program analysis, an unfamiliar reverse-engineering solve, a toy memory-bug investigation, and a fuzz/patch/regression experiment. Score: **program understanding / evidence-supported impact / experimental reproducibility / patch and honest limitations**.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 15 — Final graduation assessment

quizQuestions.prompt: How should a report distinguish “not vulnerable,” “not tested,” and “inconclusive”?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Use explicit statuses tied to evidence and coverage; an untested or unresolved case is not a clean bill of health.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should the executive summary avoid listing only CVE numbers and tool output?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Decision-makers need affected operations/data, priority, confidence, and actions; raw identifiers do not provide that context.

quizQuestions.prompt: What do you do when a promising route crosses the written scope boundary?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Stop that route, document the boundary, and request a scope decision before proceeding.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should a severe finding include a realistic business-impact scenario rather than only a score?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The scenario connects observed technical capability to the organization's exposure and decisions without exaggerating untested consequences.

quizQuestions.prompt: What evidence distinguishes your independent work from following a walkthrough?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Dated hypotheses, failed attempts, novel variations, reproducible explanations, and fresh unseen solves provide stronger evidence than flags alone.

quizQuestions.prompt: What would justify claiming advanced capability in a specialty?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Repeated success on unfamiliar problems, understanding of internals and limitations, reliable reporting, and external/peer feedback—not completing a playlist.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: score **assessment coverage / independent technical reasoning / report-and-remediation quality / professional execution** separately for each capstone. Each must pass 16/20 with no criterion below 3. A peer reproduces at least one finding per capstone when possible; otherwise perform a clean rebuild and retest after a week, labeling it self-review. Do not fabricate additional findings to meet a quota: select a lab designed to contain enough issues, and change targets if necessary. **Graduation statement:** “I can independently scope and perform lab-based web, host, network, and identity assessments; validate and report findings; and reproduce fixes. My demonstrated specialist area is ____. My remaining limitations are ____.” Replace “lab-based” with professional claims only when supported by actual authorized engagement experience.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 16 — Mobile assessment

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is an embedded application secret usually recoverable by someone who has the app?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Delivered code/resources and runtime behavior can be inspected; obfuscation changes effort, not the fundamental trust issue.

quizQuestions.prompt: How does an exported component change an Android app's attack surface?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Other apps or callers may reach it, subject to platform permissions and its own checks.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is local biometric success insufficient proof of server-side authorization?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A client result is not a server policy decision; the backend must authenticate and authorize the actual operation.

quizQuestions.prompt: Does certificate pinning fix an insecure API ownership check?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: No. Pinning constrains transport trust, whereas ownership is an application authorization control.

quizQuestions.prompt: What extra boundary can a WebView JavaScript bridge introduce?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Untrusted web content may gain access to privileged native methods if the bridge exposes them unsafely.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should Android testing not be presented as demonstrated iOS expertise?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The platforms differ in runtime, signing, storage, permissions, tooling, and testing constraints; hands-on evidence is platform-specific.

practicalCriteria.label: Fixes and scope clarity
practicalCriteria.description: Assessed as: fixes and scope clarity.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: assess an unfamiliar designated Android training app, mapping findings to MASVS/MASTG categories. Include storage, platform, transport, and API coverage with at least three validated issues and one defended boundary. Score: **platform understanding / independent evidence / backend linkage / fixes and scope clarity**. Mark iOS as conceptual unless you perform an equivalent iOS assessment.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 17 — Wireless/device assessment

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does being within radio range not authorize testing a network?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Authorization comes from the appropriate owner and scope, not signal reachability.

quizQuestions.prompt: What can a passive packet capture fail to show even when a network is active?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Other channels, missed frames, encrypted content, and unobserved time windows can hide relevant activity.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why must an enterprise Wi-Fi client validate the authentication server's certificate?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Without appropriate trust validation, the client may authenticate to an impersonating server under vulnerable configurations.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does recovering a weak test passphrase not imply every WPA3 network is vulnerable?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Protocol, handshake, protection, credential entropy, and prerequisites differ; a chosen training sample proves only its own case.

quizQuestions.prompt: What is the difference between a firmware filesystem and the running device's state?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: The image contains packaged code/configuration; runtime state adds memory, generated secrets, mounts, and configuration changes.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does a firmware update need authenticity checking as well as a checksum?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A checksum can detect accidental change but does not by itself prove who produced the update; trusted signatures establish authenticity under the key model.

practicalCriteria.label: Scope and observation limits
practicalCriteria.description: Assessed as: scope and observation limits.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: produce a wireless configuration/capture assessment and an IoTGoat firmware report with validated evidence and fixes. Score: **protocol interpretation / scope and observation limits / firmware root causes / remediation validation**. Document whether live radio and physical hardware were actually tested.
checkpoints.passRules: Quiz: score each answer 0–2; pass at 10/12 with no zero on a critical scope/isolation question. Practical: four criteria at 0–5; pass at 16/20 with no criterion below 3.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 18 — Evidence-based AI assessment

quizQuestions.prompt: Why is text retrieved from a document not equivalent to trusted system instructions?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Retrieved documents may contain attacker-controlled content; their origin does not grant control-plane authority.

quizQuestions.prompt: Does hiding a system prompt provide reliable authorization for a sensitive tool?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: No. Tool access and arguments need independent identity, authorization, validation, and approval controls.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should tenant filtering happen outside the model's discretionary reasoning?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Data authorization must be enforceable and consistent even when model instructions are manipulated or outputs vary.

quizQuestions.prompt: What distinguishes a strange answer from a security vulnerability?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: A vulnerability violates a defined protection boundary or creates demonstrated security impact under stated conditions.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why should some AI tests be repeated rather than run once?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: Outputs may vary with model behavior and context; repeated trials reveal reliability and uncertainty.

quizQuestions.prompt: What does a deterministic mock fail to demonstrate about a real model?
quizQuestions.modelAnswer: It tests integration/control logic, not the model's response distribution or susceptibility to prompt manipulation.

practicalCriteria.label: Honest limitations and fixes
practicalCriteria.description: Assessed as: honest limitations and fixes.

checkpoints.practicalBrief: submit a complete AI application threat model, two hosted-lab investigations, the 20-case evaluation set, and mitigation/retest evidence. Score: **boundary accuracy / reproducible impact / evaluation quality / honest limitations and fixes**.
